# The schema is the demo: we made four agents build the ontology instead

*Draft for the Graph Hacks blog prize. Numbers come from `docs/numbers.md` (generated by
`scripts/report_numbers.py`); rewrite in your own voice before publishing. TODO(human).*

## 1. The thing every graph demo quietly does

We built a supply chain control tower on FalkorDB first. It was good: real orders, a synthetic supplier
network, multi-hop blast radius, agents that proposed reroutes and wrote them back to the graph as auditable
actions. It had one problem, and it is the problem every graph demo has.

We wrote the ontology.

`Supplier`, `Part`, `Port`, `Lane`, `Order`. Hand-typed into a Python file, identical for every user, chosen so
that the dataset we had happened to fit it. The demo was a demo of our ontology. Show it to a shoe
manufacturer and the first honest question is: *where is "cut"? where is "last"? where is the tannery?* The
answer was a quote for a professional services engagement.

So we deleted it. All of it — the ontology, the ingest, the scenarios, the five agents, 130 Cypher files that
assumed those labels. v2 arrives with an empty database and asks the company what they do.

## 2. Four agents and a conversation

A company types a name. Then:

1. **An interviewer** — a product manager who is also a supply chain expert — asks about the business and
   works outward: products, what they are made of, who supplies that, where it is made, how it moves, who buys
   it, what the contracts promise, and what went wrong often enough that they went looking for us.
2. **A data agent** reads the brief and works out what would make it concrete, then asks for exactly that as
   **a form inside the chat** — with a repeating table for the tier-1 suppliers, days as integers, shares as
   percentages. Submit it and it comes back with a narrower round.
3. **An ontology agent** designs *their* graph model from the brief and the answers, explains it in their own
   vocabulary, and loads their data into it.
4. **An expert generator** decides which expert agents this particular supply chain needs, justifies each one
   against the ontology, and writes its system prompt.

Then you have an application. Not ours — theirs.

## 3. Four things that turned out to matter

### The agent's checklist is its working memory

The interviewer's structured reply carries `checklist_ops`: `add`, `resolve`, `revise`, `drop` against a
private list of its own open doubts, persisted as `_ChecklistItem` nodes in the tenant's graph.

This one field did more work than anything else we built. It stops the agent repeating itself. It makes the
interview as long as the business is complicated rather than as long as a fixed script. And the count of open
items is the progress signal the stage machine reads, so "are we done interviewing?" stopped being a turn
counter.

```json
{"op": "add", "id": "c6",
 "question": "BOM structure per shoe (uppers, midsoles, outsoles) and component suppliers",
 "why": "Needed for sourcing and BOM layers"}
```

That is a real op from a real run. Nobody wrote that question.

### The agent decides it is finished; the host decides whether it may be

The interviewer sets `done: true` when its checklist is clear. The stage machine refuses while
`Brief.core_gaps()` is non-empty — no products, no customers, no stated pain — and reopens a checklist item
instead:

> Before we move on I still need the basics on: movement, customers or markets. Could you fill those in?

The model is in charge of the conversation. The code is in charge of the invariant. Every agentic system we
have liked has that split somewhere, and every one we have distrusted has the model in charge of both.

### A per-tenant ontology makes Cypher's one hard rule interesting

There is no `MERGE (n:$label)`. A label cannot be a parameter. If the labels come from a model, they have to
reach the query *text* — which is the sentence that makes a security engineer put their coffee down.

Our answer has three parts. `validate_spec` rejects anything that is not a plain identifier, is duplicated,
uses the platform's reserved `_` prefix, or points a relationship at a type that does not exist. The query
text stays in `graph/queries/*.cypher`, as it always did, with `{placeholders}`:

```cypher
// kind: template
UNWIND $rows AS r
MERGE (n:{label} {{id: r.id}})
SET n += r
```

And `Q(name, label=...)` is the only function that fills them, through one regex. Everything a model wrote
goes through those three checks or it does not run. The test suite throws
`Supplier) MATCH (x) DETACH DELETE x //` at it.

### Validation is a conversation, not an exception

The first ontology an agent produces is sometimes invalid — a relationship pointing at a type it renamed, a
property type that is not in the allowed set. The first set of expert roles sometimes includes one whose
justification names no ontology type at all, which is our definition of a role that does not deserve to exist.

Neither reaches the user. The errors go back to the agent, with the list, up to twice. It fixes them. The
user is only ever asked to approve something that can actually be applied.

## 4. Two bugs we could only have found by calling a real model

We decided early that v2 would have **no fakes**: no scripted agent mode, no `FakeLLM`, no recorded
transcripts replayed as if they were a model. The suite is 191 deterministic tests that stop at the
provider boundary, plus a live suite that calls a real one.

That cost us time and it earned it back twice in one evening.

**The recursive schema.** `FormField.fields: list[FormField]` — obviously right, since a form field can be a
group of fields. Every deterministic test passed. Every live call failed:

```
claude exited 1: .../properties/fields/items must be array
```

Inlining the `$ref`s to produce a flat structured-output schema had expanded the self-reference until it hit a
depth limit and replaced the innermost `fields` with `{"type": "object"}` — a schema the provider rejects
whole. A group's columns are now a separate non-recursive type, which is also better modelling (a table inside
a table is a schema, not a form), and `json_schema` now *raises* on a recursive model rather than truncating
one. A deterministic test builds every schema the agents send.

**The free-form patch.** The interviewer sends `brief_patch` — only the fields that changed. It is deliberately
schema-free, which means it arrives in whatever shape the model found natural. Opus sent:

```json
"products": ["Runner (road running trainers)", "Trail (trail running trainers)"]
```

where a `BriefProduct` object was expected. `Brief.merge` raised, and the exception took an entire interview
turn with it. The merge now coerces what it can and drops what it cannot, and an unexpected exception anywhere
in a turn is reported in the thread instead of costing the session. A test asserts it, with the exact payload
the model sent.

Both bugs lived in the gap a fake would have hidden. We would have shipped both.

## 5. One performance finding worth the whole evening

Loading a generated ontology's instance data was taking 16 seconds for 11,500 nodes and edges. The nodes were
fast; the edges were not. The query looked innocent:

```cypher
UNWIND $rows AS r
MATCH (a {id: r.from})      // ← no label
MATCH (b {id: r.to})
MERGE (a)-[e:REL]->(b)
```

FalkorDB's indexes are **per label**. An unlabelled `MATCH` cannot use one, so each of those 5,500 rows was
scanning the whole graph twice. Grouping the edges by `(relationship, from label, to label)` — which we know,
because the batch and the approved spec both say so — and putting both labels in the pattern:

**16.3 s → 0.33 s.** Fifty times faster, for a change that is three lines and an argument to a template.
`scripts/verify_falkordb.py` checks it now, so it cannot regress quietly.

## 6. What it costs to be honest about data you do not have

A product that interviews you has an obvious temptation: when the user does not know a number, make one up.
The graph looks better. The demo is smoother. Nobody checks.

Three rules in the code, not just in the prompt:

* The data agent **must not fill a value in**. When a number is unknown it asks for a ballpark and records
  `confidence: "ballpark"`.
* The **Synthesize** button — one click, a whole form of plausible values, which is what makes the product
  demoable without a real company's data — is a *separate* LLM pass, every value stored with
  `source: "synthetic"`, rendered with a badge, and it flags the tenant.
* `source` and `confidence` are carried onto the loaded nodes, so an expert agent answering a question can say
  *"this rests on a ballpark"* — and the rule to do so is in the system prompt the host appends to every role.

And one rule in the graph: every loaded node has `HAS_PROVENANCE → _Provenance → FROM_SOURCE → _FormAnswer`.
Click any node in the UI and *"where did this number come from?"* is answered by a single Cypher query, down
to the form field or the uploaded column. That is the question every data product should be able to answer
about itself and almost none can.

## 7. What we did not build

The application that comes *after* onboarding. v1 had one — incidents, blast radius, an action queue with
human approval, playbooks that learned across restarts — and all of it assumed the ontology we deleted.

Porting it would have meant guessing what an "incident" is on a model nobody has written yet. So the plan
stops there on purpose, and the expert runtime ships with six read-only tools: describe the ontology, find
nodes, get one, walk its neighbours, aggregate a property, trace provenance. Enough for a role that did not
exist an hour ago to answer a real question from a real graph, and no more.

The next open question is the interesting one: what does a multi-hop analytical query look like over types
nobody wrote by hand? A fixed base-concept layer the generated types map onto? Richer templates? Agents
writing Cypher that is validated before it runs? We have an opinion and no evidence yet, which is the right
place to stop.
